before.title: Stress balance and finite flux on closed boxes
before.statement: Let $x$ be an inertial chart of the affine Minkowski model with coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, let $B:=\prod_{a=0}^{3}[c_a,d_a]$ with $c_a<d_a$ be a closed axis-parallel box, and let $T$ be a $C^1$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ tensor field on an open neighbourhood of $B$; put $f^b:=\partial_aT^{ab}$ (continuous on $B$) as in [[def-sr-stress-energy-tensor-and-force-density]]. (a) (Box identity.) For each $b$, with $F_a^+:=\{x\in B:x^a=d_a\}$, $F_a^-:=\{x\in B:x^a=c_a\}$ and each face integral the Riemann integral over the remaining three coordinates, $$\int_B f^b\,d^4x=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\Big(\int_{F_a^+}T^{ab}\,d^3x-\int_{F_a^-}T^{ab}\,d^3x\Big).$$ (b) (Slice balance.) Write $K:=\prod_{i=1}^{3}[c_i,d_i]$ and, for $s\in[c_0,d_0]$, $Q^b(s):=\int_K T^{0b}(s,x)\,d^3x$; this is finite and continuous in $s$. For $c_0\le s_1<s_2\le d_0$, $$Q^b(s_2)-Q^b(s_1)=\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K} f^b\,d^4x-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\Big(\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^+}T^{ib}\,d^3x-\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^-}T^{ib}\,d^3x\Big),$$ where $K_i^\pm$ are the two faces $x^i=d_i$, $x^i=c_i$ of $K$. (c) (Finite-flux conservation.) If $f=0$ on $[s_1,s_2]\times K$ and $T^{ib}=0$ on the side faces $[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^\pm$ for $i=1,2,3$, then $Q^b(s_1)=Q^b(s_2)$ for every $b$. The theorem concerns finite axis-parallel boxes in one inertial chart and is proved by the fundamental theorem of calculus. It does not assert a flux identity for arbitrary regions or hypersurfaces, does not assert that $Q^b$ transforms as a four-vector under a change of inertial chart, and asserts no conservation without the stated side-flux hypothesis; no noncompact or limiting statement is made. No choice principle is used.
before.strategy: For (a): for fixed values of the remaining coordinates, $x^a\mapsto T^{ab}$ is $C^1$ on $[c_a,d_a]$, so one-variable FTC ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]) gives $\int_{c_a}^{d_a}\partial_aT^{ab}\,dx^a=T^{ab}(d_a)-T^{ab}(c_a)$; integrate this identity over the remaining three coordinates and sum over $a$, using Fubini/iterated integration for continuous functions on rectangles ([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]], [[cor-repeated-riemann-integrals-on-rectangles]]) and integrability of continuous functions on boxes ([[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]], [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]). For (b): apply (a) to the sub-box $[s_1,s_2]\times K$ and identify the first and last faces with $Q^b(s_2)-Q^b(s_1)$ and the spatial faces with the displayed side-flux terms; continuity of $Q^b$ follows from continuity of $T^{0b}$ and the integral estimate ([[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]]). (c) is immediate from (b). Source: this is the flat finite-box flux argument of S9 of the research supplier argument, the restricted version of Crowell 9.3.2-9.3.3 pp. 192-195, with the arbitrary-region argument declined. No choice principle is used.

before.title: Hodge reconstruction of an alternating two-tensor and the optional SI field split
before.statement: Let $(V,\eta)$ be the oriented Lorentz vector space of the affine Minkowski model with orientation and volume form $\varepsilon$ of [[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], and let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be an alternating bilinear form ([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]], [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Define the Hodge dual by $(*F)_{ab}:=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ and set $(\alpha\wedge\beta)_{ab}:=\alpha_a\beta_b-\alpha_b\beta_a$. Let $n\in V$ be future unit, $\eta(n,n)=-1$, and put $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$. (a) $e(n)=b(n)=0$, and $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$ with $n^\flat:=\eta(n,\cdot)$; also $*(*F)=-F$, so the Hodge dual squares to $-1$ on two-forms. (b) In an oriented orthonormal frame with $n=e_0$: $e_i=F_{i0}$, $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$, $F_{0i}=-e_i$ and $F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$; hence the six components of $F$ are exactly the six components of the pair $(e,b)$ and the reconstruction in (a) is equivalent to these component formulae. (c) The quadratic invariants are $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|b|^2-|e|^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=-4\,(e\cdot b)$, where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are those of the spatial structure of the frame ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]); the two combinations are the independent quadratic invariants of $F$. (d) (Optional SI identification.) If in an inertial frame one identifies $F^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ for spatial vector fields $E,B$, then $e_i=-E_i/c$ and $b_i=B_i$, the invariants of (c) read $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=4\,(E\cdot B)/c$, and under the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] along $e_1$ with parameter $\beta$ one has $E'_1=E_1$, $B'_1=B_1$, $E'_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and $B'_\perp=\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$ with $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ and $v=\beta c$ along $e_1$. (e) The theorem is algebra on the oriented Lorentz vector space with the stated index and duality conventions; clause (d) is an explicitly optional identification of the components of $F$ with fields the electromagnetic framework names $E,B$, and the theorem asserts no field equation, no dynamics, no measurement and no transformation beyond the stated component law. No choice principle is used.
before.strategy: Work in the oriented orthonormal frame with $n=e_0$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]], [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c)): write $F_{0i}=-e_i$ (this defines $e_i$ through $F_{i0}$), and the spatial block determines a three-vector $b$ by $F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$; antisymmetry fixes all components. Evaluate $(*F)_{ab}=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ componentwise using $\varepsilon^{0123}=-1$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]) to obtain $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$ and the reconstruction $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$; verify $*^2=-1$ on the six basis bivectors by direct evaluation. The invariant formulas follow by expanding in this frame; the boost law follows from the tensor component law [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iii) applied to $F$ under the passive boost $\Lambda$ of [[def-lorentz-boost]] ([[thm-sr-proper-orthochronous-lorentz-algebra]]), substituting the SI identifications. Sources: the tensor component law and the Hodge-star algebra are the flat restriction of S8 of the research supplier argument; the duality conventions and the field-strength components are documented in Carroll Chapter 1 pp. 16-24 and Tong 4.5.1. No choice principle is used.

after.title: Hodge reconstruction of an alternating two-tensor and the optional SI field split
after.statement: Let $(V,\eta)$ be the oriented Lorentz vector space of the affine Minkowski model with orientation and volume form $\varepsilon$ of [[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], and let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be an alternating bilinear form ([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]], [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Define the Hodge dual by $(*F)_{ab}:=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ and set $(\alpha\wedge\beta)_{ab}:=\alpha_a\beta_b-\alpha_b\beta_a$. Use the standard form normalization $F=\tfrac12\sum_{a,b}F_{ab}\theta^a\wedge\theta^b$ in the dual coframe $\theta^a(e_b)=\delta^a_b$ of an oriented orthonormal frame, and define $(F\wedge F)(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3):=2[F(v_0,v_1)F(v_2,v_3)-F(v_0,v_2)F(v_1,v_3)+F(v_0,v_3)F(v_1,v_2)]$, the alternating four-form exterior square. Let $n\in V$ be future unit, $\eta(n,n)=-1$, and put $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$. (a) $e(n)=b(n)=0$, and $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$ with $n^\flat:=\eta(n,\cdot)$; also $*(*F)=-F$, so the Hodge dual squares to $-1$ on two-forms. (b) In an oriented orthonormal frame with $n=e_0$: $e_i=F_{i0}$, $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$, $F_{0i}=-e_i$ and $F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$; hence the six components of $F$ are exactly the six components of the pair $(e,b)$ and the reconstruction in (a) is equivalent to these component formulae. (c) The quadratic invariants are $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|b|^2-|e|^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=-4\,(e\cdot b)$, where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are those of the spatial structure of the frame ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]); also $F\wedge F=2(e\cdot b)\varepsilon$. The two scalar expressions $I_1:=\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}$ and $I_2:=F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}$ form a basis of the homogeneous quadratic polynomials in the six components of $F$ invariant under the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; the square-wedge expression is dependent, $F\wedge F=-\tfrac12 I_2\varepsilon$. $I_2$ is an oriented pseudoscalar and changes sign if the chosen orientation is reversed with the metric and $F$ held fixed. (d) (Optional SI identification.) Let $c>0$. If in an inertial frame one identifies $F^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ for spatial vector fields $E,B$, then $e_i=-E_i/c$ and $b_i=B_i$, the invariants of (c) read $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=4\,(E\cdot B)/c$, and $F\wedge F=-2(E\cdot B)\varepsilon/c$. If $\kappa:=(F\wedge F)(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(F\wedge F)_{0123}$, then $E\cdot B=-c\kappa/2$. Under the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] along $e_1$ with parameter $\beta\in(-1,1)$ one has $E'_1=E_1$, $B'_1=B_1$, $E'_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and $B'_\perp=\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$ where the cross product is the right-handed product ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), with $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ and $v=\beta c$ along $e_1$. (e) The theorem is algebra on the oriented Lorentz vector space with the stated index and duality conventions; clause (d) is an explicitly optional identification of the components of $F$ with fields the electromagnetic framework names $E,B$, and the theorem asserts no field equation, no dynamics, no measurement and no transformation beyond the stated component law. No choice principle is used.
after.strategy: First obtain an oriented rest frame adapted to $n$: the observer decomposition theorem proves $n^\perp$ is a three-dimensional positive inner-product space ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] (c)); apply finite Gram–Schmidt to a basis of it ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]) and reverse one spatial basis vector if the resulting frame orientation is negative. This uses only finite choices. Let $a_i=\theta^0\wedge\theta^i$ and $s_1=\theta^2\wedge\theta^3$, $s_2=\theta^3\wedge\theta^1$, $s_3=\theta^1\wedge\theta^2$. The declared dual and volume conventions give $*a_i=-s_i$, $*s_i=a_i$ by direct component evaluation. Thus $*^2=-1$ on all six basis forms, $F=-e_i a_i-b_i s_i$ and $*F=-b_i a_i+e_i s_i$, proving the annihilation, six-component recovery and $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$. Raise the time-spatial indices with the diagonal metric and count both orders of each skew pair to get $\frac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|b|^2-|e|^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=-4e\cdot b$. The explicitly normalized square wedge has $a_i\wedge s_i=\varepsilon$ and all unmatched terms zero, so $F\wedge F=2e\cdot b\,\varepsilon$; the witness $F_{01}=F_{23}=1$ gives $e_1=b_1=-1$ and square wedge $+2\varepsilon$. The tensor/volume laws ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] (iii),(v)) show that these expressions are invariant under proper Lorentz changes. For completeness of the quadratic invariant claim, spatial half-turns force the three coefficient blocks of a rotation-invariant quadratic polynomial to be diagonal, and proper axis permutations force scalar diagonals; it has the form $A|e|^2+B|b|^2+C e\cdot b$. For $e=(0,1,0),b=0$, an axis-one passive boost gives $e'=(0,\gamma,0),b'=(0,0,\gamma\beta)$; invariance gives $A(\gamma^2-1)+B\gamma^2\beta^2=0$, whence $A+B=0$ for any nonzero allowed $\beta$. Both surviving invariant polynomials are linearly independent by testing $b=0,e\ne0$ and $e=b\ne0$. For the optional SI identification, apply the actual passive boost matrix to the two raised indices of $F$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] (iii)). All six entries are $E'_1=E_1$, $E'_2=\gamma(E_2-vB_3)$, $E'_3=\gamma(E_3+vB_2)$, $B'_1=B_1$, $B'_2=\gamma(B_2+vE_3/c^2)$, $B'_3=\gamma(B_3-vE_2/c^2)$, which are exactly the promised vector formulas with the right-handed cross product ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Substituting $e=-E/c,b=B$ gives the displayed invariants and standard four-form coefficient $\kappa=-2E\cdot B/c$, hence $E\cdot B=-c\kappa/2$. The zero-boost case gives $\gamma=1$ directly. All arguments are finite-dimensional, choice-free algebra and assert no EM dynamics. The cached Carroll full-text equations (1.79)–(1.88), printed pp.21–23, were read for wedge normalization and the Lorentzian star-square rule; the S8 local research route is independently recomputed, not accepted by citation.

before.title: The box balance identity checked on an explicit stress-energy field
before.statement: In an inertial chart define the symmetric $(2,0)$ field by $T^{00}=x^0$, $T^{01}=T^{10}=x^1$, $T^{11}=x^0$ in the $(e_0,e_1)$ block and $0$ in all components involving $e_2$ or $e_3$ (equivalently $T=\tau^{\alpha\beta}\partial_\alpha\otimes\partial_\beta$ with $\tau$ the displayed $2\times2$ matrix). Then $f^b=\partial_aT^{ab}$ has $f^0=\partial_0T^{00}+\partial_1T^{10}=1+1=2$ and $f^1=\partial_0T^{01}+\partial_1T^{11}=0$. For the box $B=[t_1,t_2]\times[x_1,x_2]$ (with the $e_2,e_3$ intervals arbitrary, the extra face integrals vanishing) the box identity of [[thm-sr-stress-balance-and-finite-flux]]\,(a) reads, for $b=0$, $$\int_B f^0\,d^2x=2(t_2-t_1)(x_2-x_1)$$ while the boundary terms on the $x^0$ faces contribute $(t_2-t_1)(x_2-x_1)$ and those on the $x^1$ faces contribute $(x_2-x_1)(t_2-t_1)$, which sum to the same value; for $b=1$ both sides vanish, the $x^0$-face terms $\pm\int_{x_1}^{x_2}x\,dx$ cancelling and the $x^1$-face terms $\pm\int_{t_1}^{t_2}x^0\,dx^0$ cancelling. The example verifies the finite-flux identity exactly on a field with nonzero force density and no side-flux cancellation; no physical model is asserted for $T$.
before.strategy: Compute the four one-dimensional integrals on the faces with the outward sign convention of [[thm-sr-stress-balance-and-finite-flux]] and compare with $\int_B f^b$; both computations are exact, using only the FTC and the displayed constants. No choice principle is used.

after.title: The box balance identity checked on an explicit stress-energy field
after.statement: In an inertial chart define the smooth symmetric type-$(2,0)$ field by $T^{00}=x^0$, $T^{01}=T^{10}=x^1$, $T^{11}=x^0$, with every other component zero. Its force density is $f^0=2$, $f^1=f^2=f^3=0$. Let $t_1<t_2$, $x_1<x_2$, $c_2<d_2$, $c_3<d_3$, and set $A=(d_2-c_2)(d_3-c_3)>0$, $B=[t_1,t_2]\times[x_1,x_2]\times[c_2,d_2]\times[c_3,d_3]$. For $b=0$, the full four-dimensional identity of [[thm-sr-stress-balance-and-finite-flux]] reads $\int_B f^0\,d^4x=2A(t_2-t_1)(x_2-x_1)$. The temporal-face difference is $A(t_2-t_1)(x_2-x_1)$ and the axis-one-face difference is $A(t_2-t_1)(x_2-x_1)$; all transverse face terms vanish because $T^{2b}=T^{3b}=0$. For $b=1$, the temporal face integrals $\pm A\int_{x_1}^{x_2}x^1\,dx^1$ cancel, as do the axis-one face integrals $\pm A\int_{t_1}^{t_2}x^0\,dx^0$, so both sides vanish; $b=2,3$ vanish identically. For example, transverse area $A=6$, temporal length $2$ and axis-one length $3$ give bulk integral $72$ and the nonzero face differences $36+36$. This verifies the finite-box identity on a field with nonzero force density and nonzero net side flux; no physical matter model is asserted.
after.strategy: Compute all integrals as three-dimensional face or four-dimensional volume Riemann integrals. Repeated integration of each transverse constant factor gives A, then the FTC computes the remaining integrals. For b=0 the two nonzero face differences add; for b=1 the two opposite-face pairs separately cancel; b=2,3 and all transverse faces vanish. The full finite-box theorem supplies the sign convention and repeated-integration framework. No choice principle is used.

before.title: Divergence-free stress-energy with a nonconserved slice integral
before.statement: In an inertial chart define the smooth symmetric field by $T^{00}=x^0$, $T^{01}=T^{10}=-x^1$, $T^{11}=x^0$ in the $(e_0,e_1)$ block and $0$ in all components involving $e_2$ or $e_3$. Then $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ everywhere: $\partial_0T^{00}+\partial_1T^{10}=1-1=0$ and $\partial_0T^{01}+\partial_1T^{11}=0$. Nevertheless the slice integral $Q^0(s)=\int_0^LT^{00}(s,x)\,dx=sL$ is not independent of $s$: on the spatial interval $K=[0,L]$ the field has a nonzero side flux $T^{10}(x=L)=-L$ and zero flux at $x=0$, and the exact balance of [[thm-sr-stress-balance-and-finite-flux]] gives $Q^0(s_2)-Q^0(s_1)=-\int_{s_1}^{s_2}\big(T^{10}(L)-T^{10}(0)\big)\,dx^0=L(s_2-s_1)\neq0$ whenever $s_1<s_2$ and $L>0$. Thus $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ alone does not imply conservation of a slice integral; the vanishing side-flux hypothesis is indispensable, and the counterexample shows that the isolation clause of the integrated-conservation statement cannot be dropped from the integrated-conservation theorem.
before.strategy: Check the two divergence components directly; check the balance identity by computing the $x$-face integrals of $T^{10}$ over the slab, or by integrating $\partial_0T^{00}=-\partial_1T^{10}$ over $[s_1,s_2]\times[0,L]$. The construction is an explicit smooth symmetric tensor on the chart domain; it is not claimed to be the stress-energy tensor of any of the page's matter models. No choice principle is used.

after.title: Divergence-free stress-energy with a nonconserved slice integral
after.statement: In an inertial chart on all of affine Minkowski space define the smooth symmetric field $T^{00}=x^0$, $T^{01}=T^{10}=-x^1$, $T^{11}=x^0$, with every other component zero. Then $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ everywhere, since the only possibly nonzero divergence components are $\partial_0T^{00}+\partial_1T^{10}=1-1=0$ and $\partial_0T^{01}+\partial_1T^{11}=0$. For $L>0$, $c_2<d_2$, $c_3<d_3$, put $A=(d_2-c_2)(d_3-c_3)>0$ and $K=[0,L]\times[c_2,d_2]\times[c_3,d_3]$. The full spatial slice integral is $Q^0(s)=\int_K T^{00}(s,x)\,d^3x=A Ls$. The axis-one side-flux difference on a slab $[s_1,s_2]\times K$ is $\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_1^+}T^{10}\,d^3x-\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_1^-}T^{10}\,d^3x=-A L(s_2-s_1)$; all transverse fluxes vanish. Consequently [[thm-sr-stress-balance-and-finite-flux]] gives $Q^0(s_2)-Q^0(s_1)=A L(s_2-s_1)\ne0$ whenever $s_1<s_2$. For example $A=6,L=2,s_2-s_1=3$ gives $36$. Thus zero local divergence alone does not conserve a finite slice integral: the side-flux/isolation hypothesis of the integrated-conservation theorem cannot be dropped. This prescribed tensor is not claimed to arise from any selected matter model.
after.strategy: Compute the divergence components directly, then perform the full three-dimensional slice integration and the three-dimensional side-face integration. Both gain exactly the same transverse area A. The negative side-face difference gives the positive slice change through the finite-box theorem. No noncompact limit, physical model, or choice principle is used.

before.title: A prescribed covariant stress-energy tensor need not be conserved
before.statement: In an inertial chart let $\Omega$ be open and connected and let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$; define the smooth symmetric field $T^{ab}:=F\,\eta^{ab}$. Then $\partial_aT^{ab}=\eta^{ab}\partial_aF=\partial^bF$, so $T$ is conserved on $\Omega$ exactly when $F$ is constant, and for nonconstant $F$ the balance is $\partial_aT^{ab}=\partial^bF$ with nonzero four-force density. Since $\eta$ is constant in every inertial chart, the tensor expression $F\eta$ transforms covariantly under every affine Lorentz map; hence Lorentz covariance of a prescribed tensor expression does not by itself imply conservation, and the balance of an arbitrary prescribed $T$ is an additional premise rather than a consequence of its tensor character. The field $T=F\eta$ is not claimed to be the stress-energy tensor of any of the page's matter models.
before.strategy: Compute $\partial_a(F\eta^{ab})$ using $\partial_a\eta^{ab}=0$ in inertial coordinates; conservation is equivalent to $\partial^bF=0$ for all $b$, i.e. to $F$ constant on the connected domain. The covariance remark follows from [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iii) with $\eta'=\eta$. No choice principle is used.

after.title: A prescribed covariant stress-energy tensor need not be conserved
after.statement: In an inertial chart let $\Omega$ be nonempty, open and connected and let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. The symmetric type-$(2,0)$ field $T^{ab}=F\eta^{ab}$ is $C^1$, and its continuous force density is $f^b=\partial_aT^{ab}=\eta^{ab}\partial_aF=\partial^bF$. It is conserved on $\Omega$ exactly when $F$ is constant; if $F$ is nonconstant then $f$ is not identically zero, although it can vanish at some points. For the smooth explicit witness $\Omega=\mathbb R^4$, $F(x)=(x^1)^2$, one has $f=(0,2x^1,0,0)$, which vanishes on the plane $x^1=0$ and is nonzero off it. The tensor expression $F\eta^{-1}$ is covariant under every affine Lorentz change of inertial chart: for $x'=\Lambda x+a$ the scalar component is $F'(x')=F(\Lambda^{-1}(x'-a))$ and $T'^{ab}=F'\eta^{ab}$. Thus covariance of a prescribed tensor expression does not itself imply conservation; balance is an additional premise. The field is not claimed to be the stress-energy tensor of any of the page's matter models.
after.strategy: Differentiate $F\eta^{ab}$ with the constant inverse metric to obtain the force formula. Nondegeneracy of the metric makes $f=0$ equivalent to all partial derivatives of $F$ vanishing. A $C^1$ scalar is totally differentiable ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]), so the exact connected-open zero-derivative theorem ([[thm-zero-derivative-on-connected-open-euclidean-set-iff-constant]]) gives constancy; the converse follows directly. For $F=(x^1)^2$ compute $f=(0,2x^1,0,0)$, including its stationary plane. Apply the earlier tensor law ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] (iii)) with the scalar pulled back to the same physical point and $\Lambda\eta^{-1}\Lambda^{\mathsf T}=\eta^{-1}$. This proves covariance without deriving conservation. No choice principle is used.

supplier_inspections.statement_read: Let $Q=\prod_{j<n}[a_j,b_j]\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, where $n\ge1$ and every $a_j<b_j$. If $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, then for every permutation of the coordinates the corresponding repeated Riemann integral exists and equals $\int_Qf$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $F$ be a field and let $V,W$ be $F$-vector spaces ([[def-vector-space]]). For $k\ge0$, a map

$$f:V^k\longrightarrow W$$

is **$k$-linear** (multilinear) when it is linear in each of its $k$ arguments separately, with the other arguments held fixed. It is **alternating** when

$$f(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=0\qquad\text{whenever }v_i=v_j\text{ for some }1\le i<j\le k.$$

For $k=0$, a $0$-linear map is a choice of one element of $W$; for $k=1$, a $1$-linear map is a linear map. Both are alternating vacuously, because there is no pair of arguments to compare.

supplier_inspections.statement: Let (V,eta) be a Lorentz vector space. A vector v in V is timelike if eta(v,v) < 0, null (or lightlike) if v is nonzero and eta(v,v) = 0, spacelike if eta(v,v) > 0, and causal if it is timelike or null. The zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike. The sign of eta(v,v) is the causal character of v. The pairing eta itself is written <v,w> := eta(v,w) when no confusion arises. Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.

Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the affine Minkowski space, regarded as the smooth 4-manifold with its inertial atlas (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and let Omega be a nonempty open subset of A. Let r,s >= 0 be integers and let k be a nonnegative integer or k = infinity. Write T^{r,s}(V) for the real vector space of type-(r,s) tensors on V, i.e. of multilinear maps (V*)^r x V^s -> R (def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space, def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional), with the identification T_pA = V for every p in A (lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v). A C^k type-(r,s) tensor field on Omega is a map T that assigns to each p in Omega a tensor T(p) in T^{r,s}(V) such that the map Omega -> T^{r,s}(V), p |-> T(p), is of class C^k as a map from the smooth manifold Omega into the finite-dimensional real vector space T^{r,s}(V) (with any norm; finite-dimensional real vector spaces are Banach spaces and all norms are equivalent). The components of T in the inertial chart x of a frame (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) are the functions T^{a_1...a_r}_{b_1...b_s}(p) := T(p)(e*^{a_1},...,e*^{a_r}, e_{b_1},...,e_{b_s}), where (e*^a) is the basis of V* dual to (e_a). Then T is C^k if and only if all its components in one (equivalently, every) inertial chart are C^k functions of x(p), because the identification above is linear; this equivalence is the elementary form of the component law proved in thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation. A type-(0,0) field is called a scalar field, a type-(1,0) field a vector field, and a type-(0,1) field a covector field.

supplier_inspections.statement_read:
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

supplier_inspections.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space. An inertial frame of the model is a tuple (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) consisting of an event o in A and an ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) of V that is eta-orthonormal (eta(e_a,e_b) = diag(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}), future (e_0 is in C^+) and positively oriented (the ordered basis class of (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is the fixed orientation of V). Its inertial chart is the map x: A -> R^4, x(p) := E^{-1}(p-o), where E: R^4 -> V is the linear isomorphism E(u) := sum_a u^a e_a; its components x^a(p) are the inertial coordinates of the event p, and x(p) = 0 exactly at p = o. The family of all inertial frames and charts is the inertial atlas of the model; two inertial charts x, x' are related by x' = M^{-1}(x - x(o')) for M the change-of-basis matrix between the two ordered bases, so transitions are affine bijections of R^4.

supplier_inspections.statement_read:
Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

supplier_inspections.statement: Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), and let x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) be its coordinates, so that a vector is written x = x^0 e_0 + x^1 e_1 + x^2 e_2 + x^3 e_3 and the spatial part is the coordinate column x_vec = (x^1,x^2,x^3) of R^3 with its standard Euclidean structure (def-euclidean-inner-product). For beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1, where |beta| is the Euclidean norm, set gamma(beta) := (1 - |beta|^2)^(-1/2) > 1 (def-rational-power, lem-rational-power-laws). The passive Lorentz boost with parameter beta is the linear map B(beta): V -> V defined by its action on coordinates: for beta not equal to 0, x'^0 = gamma (x^0 - beta . x),  x' = x + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . x) beta - gamma beta x^0, and for beta = 0, B(0) := identity, where x' denotes the coordinates of B(beta) applied to the vector with coordinates x, and beta . x is the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) the matrix of B(beta) is B^0_0 = gamma, B^0_i = B^i_0 = -gamma beta_i for i = 1,2,3, and B^i_j = delta^i_j + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2) beta_i beta_j for i,j = 1,2,3 (with the last expression replaced by delta^i_j for beta = 0; its beta -> 0 limit is (1/2) beta_i beta_j). In the 1+1 case beta = beta e_1 this reads x'^0 = gamma(x^0 - beta x^1), x'^1 = gamma(x^1 - beta x^0). The vector beta is called the boost parameter; it is dimensionless and mathematically independent of any unit convention.

Let V be a 4-dimensional real vector space. A Lorentz form on V is a symmetric bilinear form eta: V x V -> R that is nondegenerate (both radicals are {0}) and has inertia (3,1,0): in some (equivalently, by Sylvester's law of inertia, in every) basis diagonalizing eta there are exactly three positive diagonal entries, exactly one negative diagonal entry, and no zero diagonal entry. The associated quadratic form is q(v) := eta(v,v). The pair (V,eta) is called a Lorentz vector space of signature (-,+,+,+).

Let (V,eta) be a 4-dimensional Lorentz vector space (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia) with a chosen time orientation C^+ (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets), and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model). (a) A linear Lorentz map is a linear map L: V -> V such that eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V. The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted O(V,eta). (b) If (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is an ordered eta-orthonormal basis of V (lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis), eta_0 := diag(-1,1,1,1) is the matrix of eta in it, and M is the matrix of L in that basis (def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map), then L is a linear Lorentz map if and only if M^T eta_0 M = eta_0; every linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, and the condition does not depend on the eta-orthonormal basis used. (c) A linear Lorentz map L is proper if det L = +1 and orthochronous if L(C^+) = C^+; the set of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps is denoted SO^+(V,eta). O(V,eta) is called the (full) Lorentz group of (V,eta) and SO^+(V,eta) the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; that these are groups under composition is proved in lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure. (d) An affine Lorentz map is a map F: A -> A for which there exist p_0 in A and a linear Lorentz map L with F(p_0 + v) = F(p_0) + L v for all v in V; equivalently F(p) = F(p_0) + L(p - p_0) for all p in A, and L is then unique. F is called proper (resp. orthochronous) when L is. If x is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x(F(p)) = M x(p) + b for all p, where M is the matrix of L in the frame's ordered basis and b := x(F(o)) - M x(o) in R^4. (e) In this framework, unless stated otherwise, 'Lorentz transformation' means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map; improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly (the B-page counterexample names the parity and time-reversal matrices).

Let (V,eta) be a Lorentz vector space. Vectors u,v are eta-orthogonal, written u orthogonal v, if eta(u,v) = 0. For a subset S of V the orthogonal complement is S^perp := {v in V : eta(v,s) = 0 for all s in S}, and for a vector u one writes u^perp := {u}^perp. For all subsets S the set S^perp is a linear subspace of V, S is contained in (S^perp)^perp, and S^perp = (span S)^perp; in particular u belongs to u^perp exactly when eta(u,u) = 0. Unlike a positive-definite inner product, a nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.

supplier_inspections.statement_read:
For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

supplier_inspections.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let (o;e_0,...,e_3) be an inertial frame. For v_0,...,v_3 in V let [v_j^a] be the 4x4 matrix whose j-th column lists the coordinates of v_j in the ordered basis (e_0,...,e_3), and define epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3) := det([v_j^a]) in the sense of the determinant of a square matrix. Then epsilon is an alternating 4-linear form on V, called the oriented volume form of the model. Its components in the inertial frame are the permutation symbols epsilon_{abcd}, with epsilon_{0123} = +1 and epsilon_{abcd} the sign of the permutation taking (0,1,2,3) to (a,b,c,d) (zero if two indices repeat). The raised components are epsilon^{abcd} := eta^{aa'} eta^{bb'} eta^{cc'} eta^{dd'} epsilon_{a'b'c'd'}, where eta^{ab} is the inverse of the matrix eta_{ab}; epsilon^{0123} = -1. The spatial permutation symbol epsilon_{ijk} for i,j,k in {1,2,3} is defined by epsilon_{123} = +1 together with alternation.

Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame. Put S := span(e_1,e_2,e_3) = {w in V : eta(e_0,w) = 0} and let delta be the restriction of eta to S. Then delta is a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form on S (the Euclidean spatial form of the frame), |w| := sqrt(delta(w,w)) is a norm on S, and (e_1,e_2,e_3) is a delta-orthonormal positively oriented ordered basis of S. Writing w = w^1 e_1 + w^2 e_2 + w^3 e_3, define the vector product w x z as the unique element of S with components ((w x z)^1,(w x z)^2,(w x z)^3) = (w^2 z^3 - w^3 z^2, w^3 z^1 - w^1 z^3, w^1 z^2 - w^2 z^1). Then delta(w x z, y) equals the determinant of the coordinate matrix with columns w,z,y for every y in S, and |w x z|^2 = |w|^2 |z|^2 - delta(w,z)^2. All these objects belong to the positive spatial three-space of the named inertial frame: they are equivariant under orientation-preserving spatial rotations of the frame and are not invariant under a general Lorentz map. The invariant structure of the model remains eta alone.

An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space is a quadruple (A,V,eta,C^+) consisting of: a nonempty affine space A over a 4-dimensional real vector space V (def-affine-space-and-displacement); a Lorentz form eta on V (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia); an orientation of V, i.e. a positive ray of the determinant line Lambda^4 V, fixed once and for all (def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space); and a time orientation C^+ of (V,eta) (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets). The points of A are called events; q-p is the displacement from p to q; the interval of p,q in A is I(p,q) := eta(q-p,q-p); and p,q are timelike, null, spacelike or causally related when q-p is timelike, null, spacelike or causal, future-related when q-p is future causal, and past-related when q-p is past causal (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets). No point of A is distinguished: for every v in V the translation p |-> p+v is a bijection of A preserving all the structure except the labelling of points. All later structure of this framework (frames, charts, tensor fields, worldlines) is built on this model, and no derived physical quantity is part of it.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski model, $c>0$, and let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open set. (a) A \emph{stress-energy tensor} on $\Omega$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, is a $C^k$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ tensor field $T$ on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]: at every $p$, $T(p):V^*\times V^*\to\mathbb R$ is bilinear and symmetric, so its inertial components satisfy $T^{ab}=T^{ba}$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iii)). (b) In the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] with length coordinates $x^0=ct$, the components $T^{ab}$ have the unit joule per cubic metre; the frame components are read as energy density ($T^{00}$), energy flux and momentum density ($T^{0i}=T^{i0}$) and stress ($T^{ij}$). This clause fixes a unit and a reading convention only; it asserts no measurement, no matter model and no dynamics. (c) The \emph{four-force density} of $T$ is the $C^{k-1}$ field with inertial components $f^b:=\partial_aT^{ab}$, where $\partial_a$ are the coordinate partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. By [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iv) the components $\partial_aT^{ab}$ transform as a vector, so $f$ is a well-defined vector field on $\Omega$, independent of the inertial chart. One says that $T$ is \emph{locally conserved}, or \emph{balanced}, on $\Omega$ when $f=0$ on $\Omega$, and that $T$ is balanced against the four-force density $f$ when $\partial_aT^{ab}=f^b$. (d) The definition asserts no conservation of any prescribed symmetric field $T$: whether a given $T$ is conserved, whether it arises from an action or a matter model, and whether any of its integrals over a slice converges are separate hypotheses stated elsewhere. No choice principle is used.

Let (V,eta) be a Lorentz vector space and let T := {v in V : eta(v,v) < 0} be its timelike set. By the components lemma T has exactly two connected components; a time orientation of (V,eta) is a choice of one of them. Fixing such a choice and writing C^+ for the chosen component and C^- := T \ C^+ for the other, call v future timelike if v is in C^+, past timelike if v is in C^-, future null if v is nonzero, eta(v,v) = 0 and v lies in the closure cl(C^+), past null if v is nonzero, eta(v,v) = 0 and v lies in cl(C^-), future causal if it is future timelike or future null, and past causal if it is past timelike or past null. The sets cl(C^+) and cl(C^-) are the future and past closed cones; they are convex cones meeting only at 0, and a causal vector is future or past but not both.

supplier_inspections.statement_read:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, and let $r,s\ge 0$. A
**type $(r,s)$ tensor on $V$** is a multilinear map

$$T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R.$$

With this convention, vectors are type $(1,0)$ tensors and covectors are type
$(0,1)$ tensors.

supplier_inspections.statement: Let B(beta) be the passive boost of def-lorentz-boost in an inertial frame (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3). For every beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1 the following hold. (i) B(beta) is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map: eta(B(beta)v,B(beta)w) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V, det B(beta) = +1, and B(beta)(C^+) = C^+. (ii) B(0) is the identity, and for every beta the image of the frame vector e_0 is B(beta)e_0 = gamma(e_0 - beta_1 e_1 - beta_2 e_2 - beta_3 e_3), so the map beta |-> B(beta) is injective and B(beta) fixes the origin; moreover for every vector y with coordinates (0,y_vec) and beta . y = 0 one has B(beta)y = y. (iii) B(-beta)B(beta) = B(beta)B(-beta) = identity; in particular B(beta) is invertible with B(beta)^{-1} = B(-beta), and B(beta) and B(-beta) are inverse bijections of V. (iv) If u is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates (u^0,u_vec), so that eta(u,u) = -1 and u^0 > 0, and |u_vec| < u^0, then the boost with parameter beta := u_vec/u^0 satisfies B(beta)u = e_0. (v) If a vector x has x^0 > |x_vec|, then the first coordinate of B(beta)x is gamma(x^0 - beta . x) > 0; if x^0 < -|x_vec| then the first coordinate of B(beta)x is negative. In particular B(beta) maps the future open cone {x^0 > |x_vec|} into itself.

Let eta be a Lorentz form on a 4-dimensional real vector space V. There is an ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) of V with eta(e_a,e_b) = diag(-1,1,1,1)_{ab} for all a,b. Such a basis is called eta-orthonormal; in every eta-orthonormal ordered basis exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the count is the inertia (3,1,0) of eta.

supplier_inspections.statement_read:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

supplier_inspections.statement: Let (V,eta) be the Lorentz vector space with time orientation C^+ and let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model. Then: (i) For every beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1 the passive boost B(beta) is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, B(beta)^{-1} = B(-beta), and for collinear boosts B(beta_1 e)B(beta_2 e) = B(((beta_1 + beta_2)/(1 + beta_1 beta_2)) e) for every unit spatial vector e and beta_1, beta_2 in (-1,1); in particular collinear boosts commute. If beta is the parameter of B(beta), then beta = tanh r for a unique rapidity r in R, and collinear rapidities add. (ii) SO^+(V,eta) is a subgroup of O(V,eta), which is a subgroup of GL(V); every passive boost B(beta) and every spatial rotation of the frame (extended by fixing e_0) belongs to SO^+(V,eta). (iii) Every L in SO^+(V,eta) has a unique factorization L = B(-beta) Rhat with |beta| < 1 and Rhat the extension of a spatial rotation of the frame; here beta = u_vec/u^0 where (u^0,u_vec) are the coordinates of u = L e_0. Consequently every proper orthochronous Lorentz map is the product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation (in that order), and L is itself a passive boost if and only if the rotation is the identity. (iv) Every L in SO^+(V,eta) preserves the interval eta(v,v), the causal classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the orientation and the oriented volume form of the model: epsilon(Lv_0,...,Lv_3) = epsilon(v_0,...,v_3) for all v_0,...,v_3 in V. An arbitrary element L of O(V,eta) has det L = +-1 and either preserves or interchanges the future and past cones, and det L = 1 alone does not force L(C^+) = C^+.

Let c > 0 and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space. (a) Norm of the four-velocity. Let x: I -> A be a C^1 future timelike worldline with four-velocity U (def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration). Then eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^2 for every s in I; equivalently the dimensionless four-velocity u = U/c satisfies eta(u,u) = -1, and U(s) is future timelike. Thus the four-velocity of a worldline lies on the future unit hyperboloid. (b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration. If x is C^2 at s, then eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0: the four-acceleration has no component along the four-velocity; if in addition A(s) is nonzero, then A(s) is spacelike. (c) Rest space and projection. Let n in V be future unit timelike, eta(n,n) = -1, and put n^perp := {v in V : eta(n,v) = 0}. Then n^perp is a 3-dimensional linear subspace of V, the restriction of eta to n^perp is positive definite, and the map h: V -> V, h(v) := v + eta(n,v) n, is linear, idempotent with h o h = h, has image n^perp and kernel span(n), satisfies h(n) = 0 and eta(n,h(v)) = 0 for all v in V, and every v in V has the unique decomposition v = -eta(n,v) n + h(v). Moreover |w| := sqrt(eta(w,w)) defines a norm on n^perp. (d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor. Let n and u be future unit timelike vectors, put gamma := -eta(n,u) and w := c h(u)/gamma. Then gamma >= 1, w lies in n^perp, u = gamma (n + w/c), |w|^2 = c^2 (1 - gamma^{-2}) < c^2, gamma = (1 - |w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}, and gamma = 1 if and only if u = n. The vector w is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity c u relative to the observer n and gamma is its Lorentz factor. (e) Coordinate form. Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame and let y be a C^1 future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are t |-> (c t, r(t)), with coordinate velocity w(t) := r'(t) in R^3 and, when y is C^2, coordinate acceleration a(t) := w'(t). Then |w(t)| < c, the four-velocity is U = gamma_w (c,w) with gamma_w := (1 - |w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}, and the four-acceleration is A = gamma_w (d/dt)(gamma_w (c,w)), so that A^0 = gamma_w^4 (w.a)/c and A_vec = gamma_w^2 a + gamma_w^4 (w.a) w/c^2; consequently eta(A,A) = gamma_w^4 |a|^2 + gamma_w^6 (w.a)^2/c^2 >= 0, with eta(A,A) = 0 if and only if a = 0, and eta(U,A) = 0. For the observer n = e_0 of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to gamma = gamma_w and w_rel = w. (f) Scope. The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with a fixed positive constant c; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $x$ be an inertial chart of the affine Minkowski model with coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, let $B:=\prod_{a=0}^{3}[c_a,d_a]$ with $c_a<d_a$ be a closed axis-parallel box, and let $T$ be a $C^1$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ tensor field on an open neighbourhood of $B$; put $f^b:=\partial_aT^{ab}$ (continuous on $B$) as in [[def-sr-stress-energy-tensor-and-force-density]]. (a) (Box identity.) For each $b$, with $F_a^+:=\{x\in B:x^a=d_a\}$, $F_a^-:=\{x\in B:x^a=c_a\}$ and each face integral the Riemann integral over the remaining three coordinates, $$\int_B f^b\,d^4x=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\Big(\int_{F_a^+}T^{ab}\,d^3x-\int_{F_a^-}T^{ab}\,d^3x\Big).$$ (b) (Slice balance.) Write $K:=\prod_{i=1}^{3}[c_i,d_i]$ and, for $s\in[c_0,d_0]$, $Q^b(s):=\int_K T^{0b}(s,x)\,d^3x$; this is finite and continuous in $s$. For $c_0\le s_1<s_2\le d_0$, $$Q^b(s_2)-Q^b(s_1)=\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K} f^b\,d^4x-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\Big(\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^+}T^{ib}\,d^3x-\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^-}T^{ib}\,d^3x\Big),$$ where $K_i^\pm$ are the two faces $x^i=d_i$, $x^i=c_i$ of $K$. (c) (Finite-flux conservation.) If $f=0$ on $[s_1,s_2]\times K$ and $T^{ib}=0$ on the side faces $[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^\pm$ for $i=1,2,3$, then $Q^b(s_1)=Q^b(s_2)$ for every $b$. The theorem concerns finite axis-parallel boxes in one inertial chart and is proved by the fundamental theorem of calculus. It does not assert a flux identity for arbitrary regions or hypersurfaces, does not assert that $Q^b$ transforms as a four-vector under a change of inertial chart, and asserts no conservation without the stated side-flux hypothesis; no noncompact or limiting statement is made. No choice principle is used.

Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the affine Minkowski space, let x and x' be inertial charts whose transition is the affine map x'(p) = Lambda x(p) + b with linear part Lambda (a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix by lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz), and let Omega be an open subset of A. Let J: Omega -> V, k, and T be a C^k vector field, a C^k covector field and a C^k type-(r,s) tensor field on Omega in the sense of def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space, with components J^a, k_a and T^{a_1...a_r}_{b_1...b_s} in the chart x, and primed components in the chart x'. Then: (i) J'^a = Lambda^a_b J^b: a contravariant index gains the factor Lambda^a_b, i.e. components transform by multiplication with the transition matrix. (ii) k'_a = (Lambda^{-1})^b_a k_b: a covariant index gains the factor (Lambda^{-1})^b_a. If theta(p) = k_a x^a(p) + theta_0 is an affine scalar function with constant covector k and constant theta_0, then theta(p) = k'_a x'^a(p) + theta'_0 with k' as above and theta'_0 := theta_0 - k'_a b^a, so the phase function is invariant when the constant term is transformed together with the covector. (iii) T'^{a_1...a_r}_{b_1...b_s} = Lambda^{a_1}_{c_1} ... Lambda^{a_r}_{c_r} (Lambda^{-1})^{d_1}_{b_1} ... (Lambda^{-1})^{d_s}_{b_s} T^{c_1...c_r}_{d_1...d_s}: every contravariant index gains a factor Lambda and every covariant index a factor Lambda^{-1}, and the law is consistent with the multilinear evaluation of T(p) after substituting the transformed basis. Every contraction of one contravariant with one covariant index is invariant, and the metric components satisfy eta'_{ab} = eta_{ab}. (iv) The coordinate partial derivatives satisfy partial'_a = (Lambda^{-1})^b_a partial_b wherever the derivatives exist. Consequently the divergence of a vector field is invariant, partial'_a J'^a = partial_a J^a, and for a C^1 type-(2,0) field T one has partial'_a T'^{ab} = Lambda^b_c partial_a T^{ac}. (v) Alternating covariant tensor fields transform by the covariant law on each slot; the oriented volume form of the model satisfies epsilon'_{abcd} = epsilon_{abcd}, since det Lambda = +1, whereas a general Lorentz matrix with det = -1 changes its sign. (vi) Let J be a C^1 vector field with components (J^0,J^1,J^2,J^3) in an inertial chart, and write the spatial block as J_cov := (J^1,J^2,J^3) and denote by partial_i the spatial partial derivatives in the chart. Then the continuity equation partial_a J^a = 0 is equivalent to partial_0 J^0 + sum_i partial_i J^i = 0, and under the passive boost with parameter beta (Lambda = B(beta), Lambda^{-1} = B(-beta)) the components transform as J'^0 = gamma(J^0 - beta . J_cov), J'_cov = J_cov + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . J_cov) beta - gamma beta J^0. (vii) If U is a C^1 future timelike vector field and rho_0 a C^1 scalar field, then J := rho_0 U is a C^1 vector field and its first component satisfies J^0 = rho_0 U^0; writing rho := J^0 (the coordinate density in the chart) and u := U/U^0 (the coordinate velocity), one has rho = rho_0 u^0. Coordinate density and the scalar multiplier rho_0 are different objects: they agree only in charts in which u^0 = 1. Interpretation boundary: the identification of a physical charge-current with a vector field, and of rho with a measured charge density, is a model premise of the electromagnetic framework; this item is a statement about the transformation of components of specified fields and does not by itself assert that any physical current transforms as a vector.

supplier_inspections.statement_read: Let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, open, and connected, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be totally differentiable at every point ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]). Then $Df=0$ on $U$ if and only if $f$ is constant on $U$.
